a-short-chat.content:
The dominant cost for a long prompt is the prefill phase, where the model must process the entire input sequence in parallel to compute the initial hidden states. On a single GPU with ample memory, this phase is compute-bound rather than memory-bound, meaning the time scales roughly linearly with the number of input tokens as the attention mechanism performs quadratic or near-linear operations depending on the implementation. In contrast, a short chat request has a negligible prefill cost, so its latency is dominated by the first few decoding steps, which are memory-bound and limited by the bandwidth of moving the model weights from VRAM to the compute units. This explains why operators see a stark difference: the long request pays a heavy upfront tax for context processing, while the short request jumps straight into the steady-state decoding loop.

The prefix cache can only save time if the new request shares a significant, identical prefix with a previously cached request. However, if the end of every prompt changes and the prompts are not structurally similar at the beginning, the cache hit rate drops to near zero, rendering the cache useless for these specific long requests. Reach for `Arc<RwLock<T>>` when you have many concurrent readers but rare writers, as it allows multiple threads to hold a read lock simultaneously, maximizing throughput for read-heavy workloads. This is ideal for scenarios like configuration tables or caches where the data is stable but needs to be visible to many consumers at once.

However, `Arc<Mutex<T>>` is often the better choice even for read-heavy data if the critical section is extremely short (e.g., a simple integer increment or a quick lookup) or if the read operations are not truly independent. Mutexes have lower overhead per operation and avoid the complexity of managing multiple readers, making them faster in practice for high-frequency, low-latency operations where the contention cost of an RwLock outweighs its concurrency benefits.

A small correction to the premise: a CONDITION decides whether a transition is offered at all, so it cannot enforce anything — use a VALIDATOR (it blocks the move and shows the user why). Recommended shape: statuses To Do / In Progress / In Review / Done (keep Approved as an optional extra status if you want to record WHO approved). Transitions: To Do->In Progress (self), In Progress->In Review (self), In Review->Done (self), In Review->In Progress (self, 'Changes requested'), plus a global 'Reopen' Done->In Progress. On In Review->Done set a system post-function to record the approver (e.g. set a user custom field 'Approved by' to {{reporter}} or the current user) so the audit shows who approved. Validator on In Review->Done: 'Issue Assignee' not equal to the current user (user condition on the Assignee field) — this forces a reviewer other than the assignee to approve.

(Source: support.atlassian.com/jira-cloud-administration/docs/set-up-a-workflow-validator/)
